title: Conciliation of intellect-only and both-faculties; Ames will-only improbable
source_text: XXIV. Et ita quidem conciliari possunt sententiae eorum qui dicunt fidem esse in solo intellectu, & eorum qui, contra, contendunt fidem intellectum & voluntatem occupare, & utrique facultati, tanquam subjecto inesse. Sed omnino improbabilis est sententia Amesii & eorum qui cum illo censent fidem esse in sola voluntate, cum alienum sit a recta ratione statuere fidem in assensu, saltem ex parte, non consistere, & assensum non esse fidei actum. Neque hoc statui potest, quin immutetur communis & usitata notio vocabuli fidei, quod a viro sapiente & cordato fieri non debet.
pass_a_gloss: And so the opinions of those who say faith is in intellect alone and of those who contend that faith occupies intellect and will and inheres in both faculties as subject can indeed be reconciled. But altogether improbable is Ames's opinion and of those who with him judge faith is in the will alone, since it is alien to right reason to hold that faith does not consist in assent at least in part, and that assent is not an act of faith. Nor can this be held without changing the common and usual notion of the word faith, which a wise and prudent man ought not to do.
pass_b_english: Intellect-only and both-faculties views can be reconciled by the twofold sense.
Ames's will-only view is improbable: dropping assent as faith-act rewrites the word's common sense.
